reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents an MEV bot as able to profit from sandwiching pending Uniswap transactions and directs viewers to deploy the contract and deposit at least 0.2 ETH to its contract or bot address. The narrated steps connect compiling and deploying the contract, sending ETH through MetaMask, and starting the bot, while sampled frames show the send flow and deployed-contract controls. the available video evidence does not establish actual profits, losses, contract ownership, recipient control, or whether the code performs as described.

This will make MetaMask pop up, so we have to confirm this in order for the bot to start.
You're going to have to send gas money to run this contract.

opening.argument: The presentation acknowledges meaningful downside rather than promising a guaranteed return. It warns that gas and token burn fees can consume more than the bot makes, specifically stating that a high-burn-fee target can cause the contract to waste more in fees than it earns. It frames the funding recommendation as a way to address those costs, not as a guarantee of income. That qualification matters when assessing whether the presenter is claiming certain profits.

citations.quote: If you fund the contract with 0.4 ETH or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit.
I recommend funding the contract with around 0.5 - 1 ETH just to make sure that won't happen.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution emphasizes the deposit instructions, but those instructions are accompanied by an explicit warning that costs can exceed earnings. Its slippage quote describes the proposed mechanism; it does not establish that every run will profit. The narration also says unused gas money remains in the contract. Those qualifications do not prove the bot works, but they weaken the claim that the presentation promises a risk-free return.

citations.quote: the contract will basically waste in fees more than make profit
You'll only use the amount of gas that it needs to run and you'll always have that money still left in your contract.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about fees does not neutralize the central pitch. The instructions still tell viewers to deposit ETH and present the bot as profiting from slippage. Saying unused gas remains in the contract does not establish that viewers can recover their funds, that the code performs as described, or that any profit occurs.

opening.argument: The content can be read as an operational programming demonstration. It walks through creating a Solidity file, changing the compiler version, deploying through a connected wallet, and interacting with a contract. The narration begins by saying it will show viewers how to commence a flash loan on Uniswap. Those concrete steps make technical instruction central to the video. Demonstrating a workflow does not, by itself, establish that the proposed trading strategy succeeds or that the presenter guarantees its results.

we're actually using version 0. 6.12. So we're going to have to change this.
change this to Inject Web 3.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the deployment and funding steps as a solicitation, but they are also part of the narrated procedure for running the demonstrated contract. The narration shows how to start it and describes a stop-and-withdraw sequence. Neither those steps nor the sampled controls establish a completed profitable trade. The stronger reading is a tutorial presenting a proposed mechanism, with its actual performance unresolved.

If you want to withdraw at any point, then you can hit stop, then the withdraw button.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The procedural format does not make this merely educational. The instructions direct viewers to deploy a contract, send ETH to it, and activate it, while asserting that the bot profits from slippage. Showing the steps supplies no independent verification of the code or its returns; it makes the funding request more actionable.

opening.argument: The material presents a software workflow, not a conventional managed investment account or recruitment scheme. It does not ask viewers for login credentials, promise a fixed return, or describe downline payments. Instead, it says viewers deploy a contract using their connected wallet, identifies the resulting address as their contract address, and describes a withdrawal control. Those statements do not prove the contract is safe, but the supplied material also does not establish that the presenter controls the recipient or that funds cannot be withdrawn.

citations.quote: make sure you have ETH in the wallet you have connected to remix
After the transaction is confirmed, it's your own BOT now
This is your contract address.
If you want to withdraw at any point, then you can hit stop, then the withdraw button.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a funding step, but the narration describes that transfer as gas money for a deployed contract, not a payment to the presenter. Calling it the viewer's contract and describing a withdrawal button does not verify control, yet the opening likewise concedes it cannot establish recipient control or actual losses. On this record, those uncertainties should not be treated as proof of a fraudulent transfer.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the address the viewer's contract does not establish meaningful control or recoverability. The content still instructs viewers to deposit ETH, says the bot will work, and claims profit from slippage. A missing credential request or downline does not validate the funded-contract return claim; the code's behavior and the claimed profits remain unverified.
